query: Earlier studies used carbothermal shock, fast moving-bed pyrolysis, microwave heating, polyol synthesis, and dealloying, but a straightforward, cost-effective, and scalable route remains unavailable. Prior comparative work produced sharply different outcomes among multimetal nanoparticle systems—including homogeneous alloy formation versus phase separation, elemental segregation, uncontrolled morphology, and high decomposition temperatures—without establishing a general cause. The challenge increases with more than five interacting elements and the requirement to preserve substantial surface-atom exposure for catalytic applications. Against this background, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs successful formation of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles and why? Describe one controlled comparison without naming the variable or investigative technique, predict the observations relative to an unchanged baseline, define where the hypothesis should and should not apply, relate it to the reported comparative evidence, and identify a decisive falsifying result.

generation.hypothesis: If, during the reduction of a noble metal single‐source precursor, the atomic mobility is artificially constrained such that even sequential reduction of different metal species takes place in a kinetically trapped, solid‐state environment, then the formation of homogeneous, single‐phase high‐entropy alloy nanoparticles will be favored. Conversely, if even a slight relaxation in this mobility constraint is introduced, elemental segregation (e.g., core–shell or phase‐separated structures) will emerge.
generation.material_initial_state: A well‐mixed, solid precursor comprising equimolar noble metal salts (e.g., a five‐metal single‐source precursor) deposited on a support that inherently limits atomic diffusion.
generation.intervention: Synthesize two otherwise identical batches of the precursor under rapid, low-temperature reduction conditions, with one batch processed under an enhanced kinetic trapping condition (i.e., modified thermal history that further inhibits atom mobility) and the other following the baseline protocol.
generation.conditions: Rapid reduction under solid‐state conditions at moderately elevated temperatures that allow decomposition yet avoid melting, with all variables (composition, reaction atmosphere, and duration) kept constant except for the subtle modification in the kinetic constraint on atomic diffusion.
generation.structural_mediator: The atomic-scale arrangement (degree of random alloying versus elemental clustering) within the forming nanoparticle, as determined by local bond formation and surface diffusion dynamics.
generation.mechanism: Rapid reduction produces metal atoms sequentially; however, if their mobility is sufficiently restricted by the rapid cooling and inert support environment, statistical dilution ensures that atoms randomly incorporate before they can segregate. A slight relaxation in the atom mobility permits elemental migration, leading to nucleation of element-specific clusters and eventual phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under enhanced kinetic trapping (more restricted mobility), nanoparticles will display a uniform, single-phase solid-solution with randomized elemental distribution (confirmed by high-resolution imaging and diffraction), whereas a slight increase in atomic mobility will result in detectable elemental segregation (such as core–shell features).
generation.baseline: Nanoparticles produced under standard rapid low-temperature reduction conditions, where inherent atomic mobility is limited but not maximally suppressed.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to solid-precursor, low-temperature reduction processes in noble metal HEA systems. It might not hold in synthesis routes involving complete melting or vapor-phase nucleation where atomic diffusion is inherently high.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative threshold at which atomic mobility transitions from being sufficiently constrained to allowing elemental segregation is not established. This proposal builds on the stochastic formation model described in PMC10621632 (where limited precursor mobility was key for single-phase HEA formation) and the controlled dropwise injection experiments in PMC10171813 (which highlight the impact of reduction kinetics). The new aspect is the direct test of modifying atomic mobility via subtle thermal history adjustments—a parameter whose specific range and influence remain to be rigorously quantified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of noble metal precursor samples on identical supports. Process one set using an enhanced rapid thermal procedure engineered to further restrict atomic mobility during reduction (e.g., via an optimized reactor geometry or additional thermal quench) while processing the control set under the baseline rapid reduction conditions. All other synthesis parameters (composition, temperature ramp, duration, atmosphere) remain identical.
measurements: High-resolution STEM-EDX mapping to assess elemental distribution within nanoparticles
X-ray diffraction to determine phase purity and crystallinity
Catalytic activity tests (e.g., electrocatalysis) to correlate structural uniformity with performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the nanoparticles from the enhanced mobility restriction condition do not display significantly improved elemental homogeneity (or show a similar degree of phase segregation as the baseline) as compared to the control, then the hypothesis that constrained atomic mobility governs the successful formation of homogeneous HEA nanoparticles will be falsified.

cited_evidence.kind: web:One-pot synthesis of phase-separated multimetallic nanocrystals
cited_evidence.text: The numerous Pd atoms formed from the Pd(II) reduction within a short time underwent nucleation and growth to generate nanocrystals, and, subsequently, the atoms from the other precursors [i.e., Pt(II), Rh(III), Ir(IV), and Ru(III)] with slower reduction kinetics can be deposited on the just-formed Pd nanocrystals, leading to the formation of phase-separated multimetallic nanocrystals with the Pd-rich core and Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru shell (Fig. 1, E and F). In addition, the number of nucleation sites provided by the just-formed Pd nanocrystals is not sufficiently large to accommodate all the four Pt, Rh, Ir, and Ru atoms. These four atoms can also undergo nucleation and growth to generate clusters/nanowires (Fig. 1, G and H). In addition, we obtained the phase-separated PdPtRhIrRu nanocrystals as the products using different reaction temperatures of 140°, 160°, and 200°C through the one-pot synthesis (fig. S3, A to F).

We argue that the dropwise strategy can provide an opportunity to simultaneously reach a steady state for the number of each metal precursor in the reaction solution. This may allow us to tightly control the number of atoms generated from the different types of precursors at the same value in the time interval between adjacent drops during the steady state, followed by their nucleation and then growth into HEA nanocrystals. Simultaneous in situ X-ray diffraction and multi-edge X-ray absorption spectroscopy experiments allowed us to study the formation mechanism of noble metal bimetallic and high entropy alloy nanoparticles in depth. The samples were prepared by reduction of single-source precursors. For five-element mixtures, the formation of a single phase occurs more readily than in the binary samples. Under the studied reaction conditions, single-phase formation for binary alloys was restricted to systems where cooperative reduction occurred, while single-phase HEA particles could be obtained even though the elements were reduced consecutively. The findings are explained with a stochastic model that simulates the particle formation process. Regardless of the element interactions, the model quantifies that it is more likely to form a random alloy if more atom types are present in a system with limited free atom mobility. This highlights that knowledge of the formation mechanism is crucial for understanding the material formation pathways.
